items.heading: Trains: tap and forget
items.detail: Every rail operator on this trip takes the Wallet Suica — JR and the Shinkansen gates, Keisei, Keiō, Tokyo Metro, Toei, Kintetsu, Keihan, Eizan and the Kyoto subway. Tap in, tap out, no thought required.

items.heading: Buses and trams: the door changes by city
items.detail: Every road leg on this trip carries its own instructions — open the day and read the leg. The short version: Kyoto boards at the REAR and you pay on the way OUT; Nara city buses board at the FRONT and you pay on the way IN; the Nara Kōtsū #97 — the optional loop bus on 29 October, if it is running — is the odd one out, REAR door in, FRONT door out, and TWO taps, the opposite of the Nara city buses two days later; the Hiroshima trams take two taps from any door. One vehicle on the whole trip refuses the card altogether — the Yoshino substitute bus on 5 November, which is cash to the conductor.

items.heading: Temple and shrine gates: cash, always
items.detail: Never arrive at a gate expecting to tap. Tōdai-ji is confirmed cash-only and the pattern holds across roughly forty sites.

items.heading: How much cash to carry
items.detail: Land with ¥30,000–40,000. The Narita ATMs take foreign cards, so there is no reason to buy yen at an Israeli rate. Keep the Suica above about ¥3,000 and top it up from the phone with the Mastercard — foreign Visa cards are blocked at network level for Wallet top-up, and that affects top-up only, never the Shinkansen booking. The cash fallback works on the phone card too: any Seven Bank ATM, or a konbini register.

items.heading: The four nights that need the wallet
items.detail: On 2 and 6 November in Kyoto there is no cashless path at all — first choice and backup are both cash-only. On 7 and 8 November in Hiroshima there is no credit-card path: one of the pair takes cash and PayPay, the other IC and nanaco but no cards, and 7 November's lunch is cash-only on top. Each is called out on its own day.
